Two Stage Bounded Risk Point Estimation of an Exponential Mean

Source: R/ts_br_exp_mean.R
ts_br_exp_mean.Rd

Evaluates the two stage bounded risk point estimation procedure for the mean \(\theta\) of an exponential distribution (a mean time to failure, a mean waiting time, a mean time between events). The loss in estimating \(\theta\) by the sample mean is \(A\,(\bar{X} - \theta)^2\), and the goal is a sample size at which the expected loss, the risk, is at most w whatever the value of \(\theta\). The first stage (pilot_data) fixes the total sample size; the second stage (additional_data) completes it. The estimate is the mean of all observations from both stages. The procedure is risk based, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

ts_br_exp_mean(pilot_data, additional_data = NULL, A, w, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

pilot_data

Numeric vector of the first stage observations, at least three, all positive. The whole first stage must be supplied at every call, because it alone determines the total sample size.

additional_data

Numeric vector of the second stage observations collected so far, all positive, or NULL (the default) when none have been collected.

A

The loss constant: the loss is \(A\,(\bar{X} - \theta)^2\). A single positive number, in the units of w per squared unit of the data.

w

The risk bound: the largest acceptable expected loss. A single positive number.

na.rm

Logical. If TRUE (the default), missing values are removed from both stages before anything is computed; if FALSE, a missing value is an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") (see smsd_check_methods for its print(), summary(), and tidy() methods) with columns term and value and four rows:

mean

The mean of all observations supplied, the estimate of \(\theta\).

risk

\(A \bar{X}^2 / n\): the risk \(A \theta^2 / n\) of the mean of a fixed sample of the current size, with \(\theta\) replaced by its estimate. A descriptive estimate; the guarantee is the one stated in Details.

optimal_n

The total sample size \(N\) fixed by the first stage.

current_n

The number of observations supplied, both stages together.

Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE once current_n is at least optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), loss_A, risk_bound, method, and notes (always empty for this function). There is no conf_level or width, and no variance_unusable attribute: the total sample size depends on the first stage mean, not on a variance, so a first stage of equal observations is accepted.

Details

The procedure is the two stage methodology that Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009, Section 8.3.1) attribute to Mukhopadhyay and Pepe (2006), with the improved constant that their Section 8.3.2 attributes to Zacks and Mukhopadhyay (2006). With \(m \ge 3\) first stage observations and their mean \(\bar{X}_m\), the total sample size is (the book's Equation 8.3.9) $$N = \max\{m,\ \lceil B \, \bar{X}_m^2 / w \rceil\}.$$ If \(N = m\) the first stage is enough; otherwise \(N - m\) further observations are collected, once, and \(\theta\) is estimated by the mean \(\bar{X}_N\) of all \(N\) observations. \(N\) depends on the first stage alone. The row optimal_n is this total \(N\), not the number still to collect. The constant is (Equations 8.3.11 and 8.3.13) $$B = 0.565 \times \frac{2 m (m + 1) A}{(m - 1)(m - 2)}.$$ (The book writes the rounding as one more than the largest integer below \(B \bar{X}_m^2 / w\), which is the ceiling.)

What is guaranteed. For the constant without the factor 0.565, Theorem 8.3.1 of Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009) states that the risk is at most w for every \(\theta\), every \(m \ge 3\), and every A; but that procedure uses about twice the sample size \(n^* = A \theta^2 / w\) at which a fixed sample has risk w. The factor 0.565 (Equation 8.3.13) is the improvement of Zacks and Mukhopadhyay (2006), found by exact computation of the risk; the book reports that it keeps the risk "only a shade under" the bound. That is a computed result, not a theorem, and it was recomputed for this package: the risk relative to w depends only on \(m\) and \(n^*\), and exact calculation over first stage sizes from 3 to 100 and values of \(n^*\) from 1 to 2,000 gives a largest value of 0.990 (for a first stage of 14 or 15 observations with \(n^*\) near 44). The bound holds throughout that range, with little to spare by design. The guarantee rests on the exponential model.

What it costs. The expected total sample size exceeds \(n^*\) by a factor that depends on the first stage size: about \(0.565 \times 2 (m + 1)^2 / ((m - 1)(m - 2))\), which is 9.04 for \(m = 3\), 1.90 for \(m = 10\), 1.46 for \(m = 20\), and tends to 1.13. See ts_br_exp_mean_pilot for the table and for the choice of first stage size, which the source leaves open.

The data must be positive, as exponential observations are. Data on a scale so large or so small that the square of a mean cannot be represented in double precision (a mean beyond about \(10^{154}\) or below about \(10^{-154}\)) are an error that says to express them in other units; no row of the result is ever infinite.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

Mukhopadhyay, N., & Pepe, W. (2006). Exact bounded risk estimation when the terminal sample size and estimator are dependent: The exponential case. Sequential Analysis, 25(1), 85–101. doi:10.1080/07474940500452254 (As described in Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009, Section 8.3.1, Equations 8.3.9 and 8.3.11.)

Zacks, S., & Mukhopadhyay, N. (2006). Bounded risk estimation of the exponential parameter in a two-stage sampling. Sequential Analysis, 25(4), 437–452. doi:10.1080/07474940600934896 (As described in Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009, Section 8.3.2, Equation 8.3.13.)

See also

ts_br_exp_mean_pilot for the first stage size; seq_mr_exp_mean for purely sequential minimum risk estimation of an exponential mean.

Other ts_br_exp_mean: ts_br_exp_mean_pilot()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# An operations analyst wants the mean time between service calls
# (hours) estimated under squared error loss with A = 100, keeping the
# risk at or below 4.
set.seed(113)
m <- ts_br_exp_mean_pilot(A = 100, w = 4)
first_stage <- rexp(m, rate = 1 / 2)
check <- ts_br_exp_mean(first_stage, A = 100, w = 4)
check
#> Sequential check (two stage bounded risk estimation (exponential mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 20
#>   Criterion n     : 116
#> 
#>   mean              : 1.825926
#>   risk              : 16.67003
#>   optimal_n         : 116
#>   current_n         : 20
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# The first stage fixed the total sample size; collect the remainder.
n_more <- attr(check, "criterion_n") - attr(check, "current_n")
second_stage <- rexp(n_more, rate = 1 / 2)
ts_br_exp_mean(first_stage, second_stage, A = 100, w = 4)
#> Sequential check (two stage bounded risk estimation (exponential mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 116
#>   Criterion n     : 116
#> 
#>   mean              : 1.977535
#>   risk              : 3.371244
#>   optimal_n         : 116
#>   current_n         : 116
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
